title: Traditional axiom systems are not fundamentally special; others could found new fields

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Traditional axiom systems are not fundamentally special; others could found new fields

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Apart from history, nothing fundamentally distinguishes the axiom systems traditionally used in mathematics (logic included), and many other axiom systems, often simple ones, could serve as foundations for new fields of mathematics as rich as the traditional ones.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So this leads to the conclusion that there is in a sense nothing fundamentally special about the particular axiom systems that have traditionally been used in mathematics

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 816. Scope: axiom systems underlying fields of mathematics

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-43: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.17

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is chiefly a philosophical conclusion about equivalence of foundations and unrealized mathematical cultures. Existing formal results can show similarities, but no possible corpus outcome cleanly confirms or refutes the claim as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: One could compare formal properties and research output across axiom systems, but no measurement determines fundamental specialness or the richness of counterfactual fields that have never developed.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The proposed new fields are counterfactual social developments.

"Fundamentally special" is evaluative rather than measurable.

Richness has no agreed metric.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The conclusion is that history, rather than a formal distinction, selected the axiom systems of existing mathematics, and that other systems could found equally rich fields. Richness and specialness are judgments about a practice. Sharing a formal property with a simple multiway system does not decide whether that system founds a field, so the sentence has no discriminating measurement.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Pick a formal property meant to mark the traditional axiom systems and ask whether simple unused systems share it and support a comparable body of results. The claim states no such property and no measure of richness.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Any formal property traditional systems share can be copied by another formal system, which leaves the practical claim untouched.

Fundamentally special and as rich are evaluative.
